newsitem.title: USA: Republicans begin choosing their new U.S. chairman.
newsitem.headline: Republicans begin choosing their new U.S. chairman.

text.p: Former New Hampshire Gov. Steve Merrill and moderate David Norcross led after the first ballot in the contest to become new Republican Party chairman but several more ballots seemed likely before a winner emerged.
After a bruising, sometimes dirty campaign, the 165 members of the Republican National Committee began voting in a procedure expected to last several hours, with 83 votes needed for victory.

After one ballot Merrill led with 42 votes and Norcross was second with 41. Colorado Republican State Chairman Jim Nicholson had 23 votes and Texas Chairman Tom Pauken had 22. Three others lagged behind and one candidate pulled out of the contest.
After candidates spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on campaign videos, mailings and travel, the election turned into a fight for the future direction of the Republican Party.

Carrying the banner of the right-wing and the powerful Christian Coalition was Pauken, Texas Republican chairman. Norcross, the Republican national committee's counsel, was seen as a more moderate alternative who is a qualified supporter of abortion rights.

While Republicans scrambled over the chairman's post, President Bill Clinton this week had to persuade a reluctant Colorado Gov. Roy Romer to take the job of Democratic Party chairman. The party faces a potentially damaging investigation of its fundraising practices.
Among Republicans, Merrill ran into opposition from conservatives, who said he was too closely associated with Bob Dole's failed 1996 presidential bid.

Last week all 165 committee members received unsigned mailings suggesting infidelity to his third wife forced Merrill not to seek re-election as New Hampshire governor. The mailings included photocopies of his two divorce decrees.
"Stooping to anonymous mailings doesn't help anybody," said retiring chairman Haley Barbour.
"To the degree that people are injecting crap like that into it, it's demeaning to the process," he said.

Barbour, who ran the party for four years, emerged as an influential Republican powerbroker, presiding over a campaign war chest of hundreds of millions of dollars. He also became a leading party public spokesman.
The folksy Mississippian said the fact that eight candidates were spending huge sums of money to succeed him showed the importance of the post.
"It shows the chairman's job is worth pursuing, worth the intensive effort," he said.
